The Little forest bat (Vespadelus vulturnus) is one of Australia's smallest vespertilionids, and its life-history traits reflect a classic slow-paced profile typical of diminutive insectivorous bats. Neonates emerge weighing just 1.1 grams [Wwb = 1.1 grams], a birth mass estimated from the closely related Pipistrellus pipistrellus, which is consistent with the altricial condition of most bat pups. Females eventually reach an asymptotic adult body mass of 4 grams [Wwi = 4 grams], a remarkably low figure that places this species among the lightest of the Australian microchiropterans. Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of roosting temperatures, measured at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate is 4.08 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 4.08 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that underscores the energetic economy required to sustain such a small body size. This metabolic rate sits at the lower end of the allometric scaling curve for insectivorous bats, reflecting the species' reliance on torpor during cooler months to conserve energy.

Reproductive output in Vespadelus vulturnus is characteristically low for a bat of its size, with females producing a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter]. This modest fecundity is paired with an equally restrained reproductive frequency, as females typically produce just one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. When the thermal environment is held at a stable 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], this combination of litter size and annual frequency defines the maximum reproductive rate. The strategy of investing in a single, relatively well-developed offspring each year is a common pattern among small vespertilionids, where the energetic demands of lactation and the constraints of body size limit the potential for larger litters. This low fecundity is compensated by a relatively high probability of juvenile survival, as maternal investment in the single pup is substantial.

The gestation period of the little forest bat, based on data from the congeneric Pipistrellus pipistrellus, lasts 42 days [tg = 42 days] when measured under thermoneutral conditions at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This is a relatively short gestational interval for a vespertilionid of its size, consistent with the rapid embryonic development typical of small bats that rely on seasonal insect abundance. The timing is likely synchronized with peak prey availability in late spring and early summer, ensuring that neonatal pups enter a period of high food availability. Following parturition, the single altricial neonate remains dependent on maternal milk for a substantial period. The weaning period is completed at 42 days after birth [tx = 42 days after birth] under the same thermal regime, meaning that pups are nutritionally independent by mid-to-late summer at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This interval includes the critical phase of flight development and initial foraging attempts, which are essential for survival before the onset of winter.

Sexual maturation in Vespadelus vulturnus occurs relatively late compared to many other mammals of similar size, reflecting the slow life-history pace of this species. Drawing on comparative data from Pipistrellus pipistrellus, the time from birth to puberty is estimated at 256 days [tp = 256 days] when maintained at a thermoneutral temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This timing means that young born in the summer reach reproductive maturity by the following spring, when conditions are again favorable for mating. The protracted juvenile period allows for extensive learning of foraging skills and the development of the flight musculature necessary for efficient hunting. This delayed onset of reproductive capability is a common feature among bats, where the acquisition of adult body mass and skilled aerial predation requires a prolonged period of post-weaning growth and experience. The 256-day interval to puberty is consistent with the annual cycle of temperate-zone vespertilionids.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the little forest bat has been estimated at 9.1 years [am = 9.1 years] when measured under stable thermal conditions at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This longevity is remarkable for a mammal of only 4 grams [Wwi = 4 grams] adult body mass and stands in stark contrast to the short lives typical of many similarly sized terrestrial mammals. The exceptional lifespan is a hallmark of the bat life-history syndrome, in which low extrinsic mortality from predation and the evolution of flight have favored extended somatic maintenance. Converting to calendar days, this corresponds to approximately 3321 days, a duration that allows many reproductive seasons and the potential for multiple litters over a lifetime. The combination of a single offspring per year and a long reproductive lifespan underscores a strategy of low annual fecundity compensated by iteroparity, which is typical of long-lived small mammals that face high risks of energy limitation.
